title: The most valuable nomination of all time?
subtitle: On Still Counting EP11, we talked about Jon Ossoff and the bright but uncertain future for Democrats.
contentHtml:
Ironically, because Washington is so close to New York, I don’t really see much of the city. It’s not like going to LA where, even on a work trip, I’ll plan some excursions — it’s pretty much in and out. But I did get to spend some time on Saturday, on a crisp afternoon, walking and running along the National Mall. The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool looks great, by the way; the White House does not.

I was also in DC for the 2008 presidential election, and of course there were lots of celebrations even in a famously buttoned-up town. Midterms aren’t like that and don’t trigger the same outpouring of emotions (except maybe, this year, in Austin). And that’s fairly rational, I suppose. Republicans have nothing at all to celebrate, except maybe Florida and some comparative overperformance in New England. But for Democrats, the job is only half-done. Even with large majorities in the House and Senate, Congress will serve as less of a check on a president’s power when he exercises most of his authority through executive actions anyway — and the powers of the executive branch are interpreted liberally by courts. The 2026 midterm will go down in the history books, and the election was played for keeps. Democrats will probably hold the Senate even if they lose the presidential race in two years. But the total and complete repudiation of Trump that Democrats are hoping for will require flipping the White House in 2028, too.

So in our Still Counting live show in Washington on Saturday, we talked about what the future holds for Democrats:

Audio version here. As always, we’re grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Note that this was taped in front of a live audience.

The context

You can accuse us of pandering to the crowd, but Galen, Clare, and I conducted a “mini-draft” of Democratic primary candidates. The truth is, it didn’t differ that much from our last pre-midterm draft. But this time, I was lucky enough to draw the first pick and chose who is technically the senior Senator from Georgia, Jon Ossoff. I selected his colleague Raphael Warnock with my second pick, and Gavin Newsom in the third round. (I’m not a fan of the latter exactly, but I’ll grab value when I see it.)

At prediction markets, Ossoff is now the frontrunner by some margin, with about a 1-in-4 chance of becoming the nominee — AOC is second — although traders are also not necessarily convinced that he’ll run.

There’s perhaps a little bit of a syndrome here of Ossoff having become the consensus #1 overall NBA/NFL pick with a degree of projection involved. I was going to write something about how he hasn’t really “proven” anything, but that’s inherently true for basically any potential presidential nominee. And this is not exactly a “stats vs. scouts” thing. Ossoff won Georgia by 18 points on Tuesday. Sure, in baseball terms, you can “park-adjust” that result; it was an extremely favorable climate for Democrats, who are going to win the national House popular vote by something like 13 or 14 points. He hit .370, but it was at the equivalent of Coors Field.

It was nevertheless an impressive outcome. And the man’s talents are pretty obvious. In particular, Ossoff seems roughly equally acceptable to both the moderate and progressive factions of the Democratic Party. That’s how nominations are typically won in the Democratic Party (although it hasn’t always resulted in great candidates). Ossoff easily won the Crooked Con straw poll, which, for what it’s worth, probably reflects a reasonably fair balance between the progressive and moderate factions of the Democratic Party.

Ossoff also said during the closing weeks of his campaign that he won’t run in 2028. These sorts of protestations aren’t very reliable, however. Politicians, notably including Ossoff, have big egos. He doesn’t even have the excuse anymore of potentially being replaced in the Senate by a Republican, since Keisha Lance Bottoms will become Georgia’s new governor in January.

Do I buy that he might not run? Sure, I guess. Who knows what’s in anybody’s heart. Mostly, though, I presume that people respond fairly rationally to incentives. And the 2028 Democratic nomination is an extremely desirable one, for three reasons.

  1. The “fundamentals” are strong for Democrats.

At prediction markets, Democrats are roughly 2-to-1 favorites to win in 2028.

This is a slightly uncomfortable fact. 2-to-1 is a pretty bold forecast; it’s not 55/45 or 60/40. The heuristic that presidential elections should basically default to a toss-up in the absence of polls or other information is usually hard to beat. On top of that — and we’ve been guilty of this ourselves sometimes — there can be a tendency to project forward from the most recent election result, when the boring bet of mean reversion is usually more reliable in the long run. Presidential elections in the modern American system are typically highly competitive. It’s easy to imagine any number of ways in which things could go poorly for Democrats, including by choosing a “bad” nominee.

I’m not sure I want this to turn into the official “does Nate really think Democrats are 2:1 favorites in 2028 given current conditions?” post. I need to think more about it. For instance, I want to think about Democrats’ state-by-state performance and consider whether that implies any sort of Electoral College disadvantage — or perhaps even an advantage. One of the few bright spots for Kamala Harris in 2024 was that the Electoral College/popular vote gap closed significantly. She lost the tipping-point state, Pennsylvania, by 1.7 points, essentially the same as her 1.5-point overall loss to Trump in the national popular vote. Part of that was because Democrats’ biggest declines, and Trump’s biggest gains, came in places like New York City where Democrats can afford to hemorrhage voters because they’ll win still by humongous margins instead of spectacularly humongous ones. In a Moneyball sense, that makes for a more efficient coalition, since you don’t have quite as many wasted votes.

Still, I’ve probably already tipped my hand on this question. I think the 2006/2008 precedent is quite relevant. Among the famous recent-ish midterm landslides, only 2006 featured a true lame-duck president. And the election two years later went about as well as possible for Democrats; Barack Obama even won Indiana.

It’s not necessarily impossible to imagine President Trump becoming a bit more popular by 2028, particularly if partisan motivated reasoning kicks in. But it is hard to see him becoming outright popular, especially since the internals on his approval ratings — only 20 percent of Americans strongly approve of the president’s performance — are actually worse than the headline numbers. It’s also hard to imagine the Republican nominee in 2028 fully distancing himself from Trump’s shadow.

Still, there are very likely to be wild twists and turns that nobody anticipates.

But at the very least, 2028 is a highly winnable election for Democrats. If you’re on the fence between running and not running, there might not be a better opportunity any time soon.

  1. If Democrats win the presidency, the president will probably command fairly large congressional majorities.

We covered the 2028 Senate outlook in Friday’s newsletter. Democrats are probably going to wind up with 56 Senate seats this year. It would likely take a Republican landslide in 2028 to reverse that majority in the span of a single election.

Humility would say not to rule a GOP landslide out, but I think that’s a less likely outcome than a narrow GOP win, a narrow Democratic win, or a D landslide. Even under a 2024-like scenario, Democrats would probably hold their Senate majority. And in the latter two scenarios, they might expand it.

The House is a different question. In the Senate, two-thirds of the seats hold over from year to year. Maybe FLIPR will annoy our bluer subscribers that year, but look, 2032 might be a rough year for Democrats, and incumbents like Scott Colom in Mississippi are going to be extremely vulnerable. But that’s six years away and, presuming Colom is eventually declared the winner, he’s earned his Senate seat until then.

In the House, everyone comes up for election every two years, however. What long-term gains do you lock in by winning? Not necessarily that many, although there are some.

The incumbency advantage, however diminished it is, is probably still a net-positive: you can look at an election like 2012 when Obama had a pretty great year but Democrats didn’t come particularly close to flipping back the House after their disaster in 2010. The other long-term benefit would be to lock in some gains from redistricting, which is now an every-two-years thing instead of once a decade.

I’m not sure I’ve fully processed the implications of 2026 for state legislatures and so forth, other than that they’re obviously directionally favorable for Democrats. It’s not strictly impossible that Democrats win the presidency by say 1 point in 2028 but lose control of the House; that would be one of those FLIPR-ish outcomes that nobody necessarily “buys”. Nevertheless, a trifecta is likely if not certain conditional upon a Democrat winning the presidency.

  1. The opportunity to define the Democratic Party

To a first approximation, one might say that American political parties are defined through presidential nominations. But there are times when the parameters are a little more open, and this looks like one of those years on the Democratic side.

Isn’t 2028 going to be an existential nomination for the GOP too? Trumpism/MAGA versus some Whole New Thing is as existential as it gets. I’m just not sure how easy it will be to create the Whole New Thing by 2028. A “45-degree pivot from MAGA” seems like the game-theory equilibrium. That might produce a little bit of a “lipstick-on-a-pig” nomination for Republicans when it takes until 2032 for the party to rid itself of Trumpism.

Still, the Democratic Party is fairly leaderless and rudderless at the moment. In a weird way, that might have been an advantage last Tuesday. The party basically nominated a bunch of normal-seeming people who were reasonably well-curated for their local environments, while Republicans didn’t. In presidential years, though, you have to stand for something, not just against something. It’s not obvious what Democrats stand for exactly, but the 2028 nominee is going to have a lot to say about that.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

The pace of newsletters is going to slow down soon enough, though we’re not done reflecting on 2026. I’m also thinking it might be a good time for our much-belated update to our Jan. 2025 post, 113 predictions for Trump’s second term.

I also don’t want to wait too long before digging in on our next big modeling project, rebooting our NBA projection system, a.k.a. RAPTOR 2.0.

And we’re probably going to be posting a job listing or two soon. Look, we’re always amazed by how much support we get from you subscribers and feel incredibly lucky and privileged for it. We think it makes sense to continue investing in the product to hopefully give you an even better and more robust Silver Bulletin experience. We’re not quite sure about how we want to go about doing this, but we figure Silver Bulletin has probably grown out of the “three kids in a trench coat + an NCAA tournament model” stage.
